item.title: Breaking Out of the Sleep Anxiety Spiral
item.description:
Some people get to a certain age, and they realize that they have been exhausted for months or even years. Sleep loss affects an array of people, from teens in the middle of exams, new parents adjusting to the demands of an infant, or elderly people dealing with rapid changes in their lives. Some people are simply tired because events like these are demanding, but many people are tired because they have sleep anxiety.

Sleep anxiety is not the same as insomnia; it is the things that cause insomnia. It is the fear you start to feel as bedtime nears, as you worry that you will not fall asleep. It is the dread you feel when you wake up in the middle of the night and see that it is only midnight. You spend hours in bed, willing yourself to sleep, but failing. You can’t help but think about your day tomorrow and the consequences of losing sleep.

Sleep anxiety is debilitating, but it can be fixed without medication or substances. Studies have shown that medication does not help with sleep anxiety in the long-term. When you begin to understand what is going on in your head and in your body, you will begin to unpack some of the anxiety surrounding your sleep problems, breaking the sleep anxiety spiral. Your overthinking might be the thing driving your sleep anxiety, but your mind is also the solution.

The Sleep Anxiety Spiral

The most frustrating thing about sleep anxiety is that it is self-perpetuating. You stress about not being able to fall asleep or stay asleep, and it is that stress that causes sleeplessness. It is like being so afraid of failing your driving test that you cannot concentrate and end up failing the test. It is a form of self-fulfilling prophecy.

Sleep anxiety doesn’t only cause you stress in the evenings, but it also affects your daytime routine. Many people believe that they can only function properly on eight solid hours of sleep per day. This is a common idea that intensifies sleep anxiety. It looks like this: you believe that you need eight hours of quality sleep per day, and so you become anxious that you won’t get that. Then it is your anxiety over not getting enough sleep that becomes the very thing preventing you from getting enough sleep.

There are things you can do and things you must keep from doing to break the sleep anxiety spiral. Overall, you must change your approach to sleep, change the way you think about sleep, and make some changes to your routine. By interrupting your thoughts and behavior this way, you are creating a new pattern for yourself, and it can adapt to your new lifestyle.

Things You Must Do to Interrupt Sleep Anxiety

There are several practical things that you can start doing to interrupt the sleep anxiety spiral. It is a good idea to speak with a doctor or specialist before starting this new regimen, or with anyone who can keep you accountable and provide support. These ideas range from simple tips to deeper and broader attitude changes.

Firstly, create a healthy bedtime routine and stick to it. Your body has a function called the circadian rhythm. This is a set of automatic responses that your central nervous system performs throughout the day to help you. When your brain registers that it is nearing bedtime, it will release a hormone called melatonin into your nervous system. This hormone brings down your cortisol levels, puts your bladder and bowels on pause for the night, and generally prepares your body to be inactive for the next eight to ten hours.

You can help your circadian rhythm in practical ways by following a 3-2-1 principle. Have your final meal of the night three hours before bedtime, have your final drink two hours before bedtime, and reduce screen time for the last hour before bed. This will prime your body for sleep even if your mind is overactive.

With sleep anxiety, you struggle to fall asleep, and you struggle to stay asleep. The first thing most people do when they wake up is to look at the clock and calculate how many hours of sleep they have left. Try taking away your ability to time-check. Remove clocks from your bedroom and place your phone far away from your bedside. This interrupts the compulsive time-checking and the anxiety that comes with it.

In a larger sense, you must change the way you think about sleeping. For example, you might believe that you can only function during the day if you have had more than six hours of sleep the night before.

The truth is that you can be perfectly functional on minimal sleep, even over a long period of time. New parents experience years of sleeplessness and still manage to get by successfully. Sometimes it is your internal beliefs about sleep that contribute the most to sleep anxiety.

Lean into the idea that you are going to be tired tomorrow, and that it’s okay. Accept whatever amount of sleep you get, whether it’s only a few solid hours. Think of nighttime as rest time rather than sleep time.

The fact that you are lying down in a relaxed, safe environment and not looking at screens is enough for your body; sleep would be a bonus. When you change the way you think about sleep, sleep anxiety begins to lose its footing and influence over your mind.

Things to Avoid While Dealing with Sleep Anxiety

It’s natural to feel helpless and overwhelmed with sleep anxiety, and many people resort to using medication and substances like alcohol to cope. These things might help get you some sleep occasionally, but there is a real danger of becoming dependent on them over time. If you have been using medication or substances to help with sleep anxiety, aim to stop using them entirely.

Avoiding screen time before bed and keeping clocks out of sight is good, but it’s also a good idea to get up if you wake up at a certain time. When you lie in bed chasing sleep, you tend to begin overthinking and stressing.

You could try using mindfulness techniques or tools like brain shuffling to get back to sleep, but it’s a better idea to get up and go to a quiet spot in the house for some reading or crafting. Try to avoid screens still, and it’s best not to eat or drink anything. Instead, doing a relaxed activity in a dimly lit room will help keep the anxiety at bay. Eventually, you will become sleepy again, at which point you can simply return to bed to sleep.

Many sleep-tracking apps try to address insomnia, but these have the opposite effect on sleep anxiety. When you have a visualization for how much sleep you’re not getting, that intensifies the anxiety you feel. The goal is to be rested, not to get the perfect amount of sleep each night. Avoid tracking your sleep or trying to meet sleep goals. Instead, aim to have a restful evening. If you fall asleep for a few hours, that’s great. If you don’t, it’s not the end of the world.

Sleep anxiety is difficult, but it’s a cycle you can break. It might not happen overnight, but if you can get to a place where you feel more rested and less anxious, you will have made incredible progress. Give yourself a break because you deserve it.

Some things are easier to face and overcome with someone on your side. Consider meeting with a counselor if your sleep anxiety has become overwhelming. If you don’t have a counselor, we hope that you can find someone suitable in our online catalog or by enlisting the help of our reception team.

item.title: Finding Freedom from Fear: A Christian Counselor’s Personal Story
item.description:
Fear is an essential survival mechanism that elicits both physical and emotional reactions. When you sense a threat, fear is protective. However, fear can be overwhelming if it is out of balance and out of proportion to the risks. Maintaining psychological balance requires an understanding of the nature of fear and practical coping strategies.

For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power and of love and of a sound mind – 2 Tim. 1:7, NKJV

My Journey Into Fear

Personally, I spent years living in fear. As a child, I was afraid of the dark. Fear followed me into adulthood, marriage, moving to a bigger city, then motherhood, and my home. Although I loved God and trusted Him, I couldn’t seem to silence the constant “what ifs” that stole my peace.

One thing that magnified my fears was the news. As long as I can remember, I’ve noticed a trend on the news and then eventually on social media: fear.

There is always something on the news or happening in the world that could make us fearful: wars, pandemics, health issues, job insecurity, the health and welfare of our children, other anxieties and phobias, etc. I got sucked into the news after 9/11. So, in 2020, after the news of the pandemic, I had to stop watching or reading the news.

I had faith; I believed in God, and deep down I knew He would protect us. But I couldn’t shake that grip that fear had on me. I would pray over our house, walk around and pray over our property, etc., but nothing seemed to help the fear subside.

I had trouble sleeping because of my fears of someone breaking into our home. I bought a little picture of an angel guarding a child’s bed and every night began to recite the passage that was printed on it: Psalm 4:8, “In peace I will lie down and sleep, for you alone, LORD, make me dwell in safety.”

I had been reading The Power of a Praying Parent by Stormie Omartian and read the chapter on fear, not just for my daughter, but for me. It was pretty humbling. I tried to read other books on fear, but they all dealt with things such as stage fright, asking for a raise, etc. Those are still real and debilitating fears, but I felt like I was the only person who was fearing for my life.

A Prisoner of Fear

Looking back, I realize I was truly a prisoner to my own mind and emotions. On top of the fear, I was dealing with so many other “issues.” God began to slowly peel away at those issues one by one, but it truly took faith to overcome the fear.

Neil T. Anderson (2017) reminds us, “Fear is a God-given natural response when our physical or psychological safety is threatened. Fear always has an object, that is something or someone, and that object must be both present and potent, that is perceived to have some power over us. It ceases to be a fear object when only one of those attributes is eliminated” (p. 28).

He goes on to explain, The fear of people, death, and Satan is the root of almost all fears. Death is still present since it is a real possibility, but once we believe in Jesus and accept Him as our Lord and Savior, it is no longer powerful (1 Cor. 15:54-55).

Although fear is a normal human reaction, sometimes anxiety and fear become more than occasional worry. I realize that, for some individuals, anxiety can involve biological, psychological, and environmental factors that require additional support. But for now, I am talking mostly about fear that is out of balance and has no real threat.

In counseling, we often talk about how our thoughts influence our emotions and behaviors. Fear thrives on repeated messages of danger, while faith grows when we intentionally focus on truth. Another perspective that helped me was understanding fear as misplaced faith – placing belief in what might go wrong rather than in God’s promises.

Looking back, I can see how fear grew stronger when I repeatedly focused on threatening information. The more I watched the news and imagined worst-case scenarios, the more my mind became trained to anticipate danger.

The Nature of Fear

As a counselor, I have seen how anxiety can affect even the strongest believers. Experiencing anxiety does not mean someone lacks faith, nor does seeking counseling, medical care, or medication indicate spiritual weakness.

God often works through the wisdom, support, and resources He provides through others. Just as we seek treatment for physical illnesses, there are times when receiving professional support for our mental and emotional well-being is an important part of healing.

One resource God used during my journey was a small booklet called Freedom From Fear. While I don’t believe one book is the answer for everyone, God used its biblical perspective to help me recognize how fear had shaped my thinking. For some reason, reading it made that little lightbulb in my brain turn on. I had that “Aha” moment.

“There are two spiritual laws at work in the world today: the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus and the law of sin and death. The force of faith comes from life. The force of fear comes from death” (back cover). In the booklet, the law of reciprocals (“corresponding, but reversed or inverted” principles) is discussed in Romans 8:2: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death.”

Understanding that fear is just faith perverted (by Satan) opened my eyes. Satan is “limited to the forces of the world.” He cannot create or come up with new ideas. He just perverts the spiritual laws that are already in place. “Sin was not a new law. It was righteousness perverted. Death was life perverted. Hate was love perverted. Fear was faith perverted (pg. 5).”

In the Garden of Eden, after Adam and Eve sinned, the first words Adam spoke to God were, “I was afraid” (Genesis 3:10). The enemy is here to steal, kill, and destroy. So, he took the faith that Adam had, and it was turned to fear. I love where it’s explained, “The counterfeit never is as powerful as the real thing” (pg. 7). Therefore, we know that when we put faith to work, “it will always overcome fear.”

The Complexity of Anxiety and Fear

As I reflect on those years, I also recognize that fear and anxiety can be complex. While my journey involved learning to trust God more deeply and renew my mind with His Word, I realize that not everyone experiences fear in the same way.

Some people have lived through traumatic events, loss, abuse, or other painful experiences that leave their nervous system on high alert. Others struggle with anxiety disorders, panic attacks, obsessive thoughts, or other mental health concerns that involve biological, emotional, and environmental factors.

Practical Steps When Fear Feels Overwhelming

  • Identify the fearful thought.
  • Ask whether there is evidence of an actual present danger.
  • Compare that thought with God’s truth in Scripture.
  • Pray honestly about your fears.
  • Pray specific and related scriptures out loud (I will list some below).
  • Reach out to trusted believers or a counselor when fear becomes persistent or overwhelming.
  • Limit media that continually fuels fear.
  • Remember that courage often means moving forward while still feeling afraid.

For me, freedom came through prayer, Scripture, renewing my mind through books and other resources, and learning to trust God’s promises. For others, that journey may also include counseling, support groups, trauma work, medical care, or a combination of these resources. God can use all of these tools as part of His healing process.

But in our everyday Christian walk, we have to walk by faith. In doing so, we have to know the Word of God and stand on its principles. We have to know that Satan is under our feet because of what Jesus has done for us. As believers, we are free from every part of the curse.

So, why do we allow him to pull us around on strings of fear, worry, anxiety, depression, etc.? Yes, we are physical beings and will have physical problems, but God is bigger than any of our problems, and He has put other people – professionals – here on earth to help us walk through some of the pains of life.

Even though we know these truths, many of us still wrestle with fear, worry, anxiety, and discouragement. Sometimes these struggles are connected to painful experiences, ingrained thought patterns, or circumstances beyond our control. Yet God’s promises remain true. He meets us in our struggles and patiently helps us grow in faith as we learn to trust Him more fully.

For believers, Scripture is the foundation for confronting fear – both the fears rooted in reality and the ones shaped by our thoughts and emotions. God can also place different resources in our paths to help us confront fear and work through the layered process of renewing the mind. We can’t just stop at reading the Scripture; we have to believe it and apply it.

James 1:22 tells us, “But don’t just listen to God’s word. You must do what it says.” We have to speak the Word and believe what we are saying. When we speak His promises, we must remember the authority that we have through Jesus and speak it with confidence, not with hesitation.

As believers, we must take every thought captive (2 Cor. 10:5). Then, we must renew our minds with the Word of God (Rom. 12:2). I will share some of my favorite passages below. 365 references in the Bible say or address, “Do not fear.” Or as one of our friends says, “One ‘Do not fear’ for every day of the year!” (I love that!)

After I read Freedom from Fear, I knew that things were beginning to change in my thought life, but it wasn’t until a women’s retreat (my first retreat with my church) that I truly became free and broke off the chains of fear. I had gone to get away, enjoy myself, and, of course, for the great teaching I would receive, but I didn’t realize it would be life-changing.

I went away still battling fear, but returned home freed from the hurts, bitterness, worry, and the rest of the lies the enemy had been telling me at that time.

Fear once dictated many of my decisions, stole my peace, and kept me awake at night. Today, I still face circumstances that could make me fearful, but I no longer live under fear’s control. Freedom did not come overnight; it came through renewing my mind with God’s Word, learning to trust Him more deeply, and choosing faith one step at a time.

Anderson (2017) says, “Courage is not the absence of fear. Courage is choosing to live by faith and doing what is right in the face of perceived fear-objects. Behind every irrational fear is a lie, which must be identified. Ask the Lord to reveal to your mind the nature of your fears and the irrational lies that compel them” (2017, p. 28).

If fear has become a constant companion in your life, know that you are not alone. Whether through prayer, Scripture, counseling, supportive relationships, or a combination of these resources, healing is possible. The Lord is for you. And because He is for you, fear does not have to have the final word.

As I’ve shared, freedom from fear did not happen overnight for me. It was a process of learning to recognize fearful thoughts, replacing them with truth, and choosing – sometimes moment by moment – to trust God. Healing often works the same way. It may involve different resources that God provides. While the journey looks different for each person, we can take comfort in knowing that God walks with us through every step.

Bible Verses to Ponder

The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? When evildoers came upon me to devour my flesh, my adversaries and my enemies, they stumbled and fell. Though a host encamp against me, my heart will not fear; Though war arises against me, in spite of this I shall be confident. – Psalm 27:1-3, NKJV

The LORD is for me; I will not fear; What can man do to me? – Psalm 118:6, NASB

Don’t be afraid of those who want to kill your body; they cannot touch your soul. Fear (reverence) only God, who can destroy both soul and body in hell. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. so do not fear; you are more valuable than many sparrows. – Matthew 10:28, 30-31, NLT

Since the children have flesh and blood, he too shared in their humanity so that by his death he might break the power of him who holds the power of death – that is, the devil –  and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death. – Hebrews 2:14-15, NIV

Seeking support is not a sign of weak faith. God often works through the wisdom, support, and resources He provides through others. Please give our reception team a call and schedule an appointment.

References: 
Anderson, N. T. (2017). The steps to freedom in Christ: A biblical guide to help you resolve personal and spiritual conflicts and become a fruitful disciple of Jesus. Bethany House Publishers
Kenneth Copeland. (1997). Freedom from fear. Kenneth Copeland Publications.

item.title: Overwhelming Anxiety in a Time of War: Finding Solid Ground Through Faith
item.description:
Here we are again. Breaking news, a new conflict has erupted in a distant land. We are glued to our televisions, computers, or smartphones, drawn in by a relentless news cycle that bring the unnerving feeling of uncertainty in a world that seems to be in constant turmoil.

As a chaplain in the Army Reserves and throughout my 21-year Army career, the all too familiar phone calls from friends and loved ones panicking over a news story of new conflict have been a frequent reminder that overwhelming anxiety during times of war impact those I love the most more than me.

We live in an age when technology keeps us connected to conflicts, even though they happen far away. We find the weight of what’s unfolding in the world, settling into our homes as if it is there to take charge. This can bring about anxiety, especially during war.

Wartime stress isn’t confined to the battlefield or the families waiting by the phone. It will creep into ordinary life, the grocery store, the drive to work, and even in the moments before sleep. Overwhelming anxiety in the middle of a global conflict is real, valid, and something that far more people of faith grapple with than most of us are willing to admit.

Wartime stress can feel invisible from the inside, even as everything on the outside looks completely normal. We go to work. We show up for our family and sit in the pews on Sunday morning. In fact, as pastor of a local church, there have been times when I have to walk in on a Sunday morning with more questions than answers about conflicts erupting around the world.

At times I wonder, Will it be me called up to go next while at the same time trying to reassure my family, friends, and congregants? The reality is that underneath all the functioning is something that feels increasingly fragile. If you feel like this, you’re not alone, and you’re not without hope.

The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. – Psalm 23:1–3, ESV

What Wartime Stress Actually Does to You

Our nervous system was not designed to absorb a continuous stream of crises. Still, with today’s technology, that is what happens: conflict dominates the news cycle and social media feeds. It leads to the sense that the world is unstable. Even though we’re not in a war zone, our bodies respond to this threat in measurable ways.

Our sleep becomes unreliable, and our concentration slips. We find that we’re easily startled and emotionally short-tempered with the people we love at the end of the day. We are exhausted beyond the point where rest can fix it. We find ourselves constantly hooked on scrolling through the feeds for updates and news.

We think that being constantly informed is a way of restoring a sense of control, even when we have no direct connection to the conflict. Compassion fatigue and secondary trauma are real. The grief we experience when we watch human suffering from a distance lands somewhere in the body and the mind, and does not dissolve simply because you step away from the computer or set down the phone.

For Christians, there’s an additional weight that comes in the quiet voice whispering that feeling afraid means you’re not trusting God. This internal pressure adds to the weight of the stress that we already carry simply because we care. Even in this, we can rest in God’s protection:

For he will hide me in his shelter in the day of trouble; he will conceal me under the cover of his tent; he will lift me high upon a rock. – Psalm 27:5, ESV

When Overwhelming Anxiety Becomes a Daily Reality

There is a difference between feeling concerned about what is happening and feeling consumed by it. Overwhelming anxiety goes past awareness and into something that disrupts our ability to engage in our daily lives. We wake up dreading the day before it has even begun. When joy feels completely inaccessible, we find ourselves mentally rehearsing a worst-case scenario in a loop that runs on its own, whether you want it to or not.

Military families, people connected to the conflict, or those who carry unresolved trauma from their own history find that wartime news triggers responses that reach well beyond ordinary worry. The result is that our minds draw connections between what is happening in the present and old wounds that were never fully healed. Suddenly, what we see unfolding across the world feels personal.

The Place Where Faith and Mental Health Meet

Some faith communities believe anxiety is a spiritual problem. The mindset in some of these communities is that praying more, studying the Bible more, and trusting God more will remove the fear that wartime news has created. Spiritual disciplines are valuable, and Scripture speaks to anxiety. The writers of the Psalms were not strangers to wartime, grief, or despair. It was all brought before God, honestly and openly, and without the performance of having it all together.

Anxiety is not eliminated by faith, but the foundation of faith does not shift when everything around you does. Faith offers a perspective that goes beyond the present moment into something eternal. It connects us to a body of believers who are meant to carry each other through the hard seasons. Christian counselors work in a way that integrates the realities of spiritual and psychological thought processes and understand that both matter.

With support, you can learn to handle your anxiety. The key is knowing what to do with it.

Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus. – Philippians 4:6–7, ESV

Finding Your Footing: Practical Steps Toward Overwhelming Anxiety Relief

Navigating overwhelming anxiety is not a one-size-fits-all process. Several practices can help us navigate a world where news is accessible every hour of the day. The first step is to limit our consumption to a defined window during the day and allow our nervous system to settle.

Making time for physical movement helps the body process stress hormones instead of accumulating them. Practices that ground us and redirect our attention to what is present and immediate interrupt the mental loops that keep anxiety running.

During a season of sustained stress and isolation, connection matters. Having honest conversations with a trusted friend or a small group that is not afraid of hard questions can build a defense against the feeling of impending doom.

Christian counselors understand the intersection of faith and mental health. They can encourage you to name what you’ve been quietly carrying. This is the first real step toward something better. Reaching out for help can be difficult, but it is a courageous step toward releasing wartime anxiety.

Hope When You Battle Anxiety

The world has had its share of war, and each generation has faced the challenge of living faithfully amid it. This doesn’t make it easier, and it doesn’t reduce the anxiety or lessen the weight of concern. But it does mean that each of us is not the first person to bring fear and faith into the same room and ask God how to handle them both.

We’re not spiritually deficient or failing. We are human, and we are living through a season that is asking a great deal of each of us.

The great thing is, we don’t have to figure it out alone. There is grace in asking for help from God, who holds all things, and from Christian counselors who are trained, compassionate, and ready to walk alongside us. The possibility of healing from wartime stress and anxiety is in process, and it is in reach no matter when we decide to begin.

If you are experiencing overwhelming anxiety related to wartime stress, or you have a loved one who is grappling with it, there are people to help. Daily life doesn’t have to feel difficult, regardless of what’s happening in the world. You can contact our reception team to schedule a time to meet with a counselor who can help you navigate this season of anxiety.

The Lord your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing. – Zephaniah 3:17, ESV

item.title: Understanding the Types of BPD and Their Connection to Substance Abuse
item.description:
Borderline personality disorder (BPD) affects how individuals experience themselves and relate to the world around them. Seeking relief from the emotional intensity that comes with BPD, individuals sometimes turn to substance abuse as a common coping mechanism. To understand why some people find themselves caught in patterns that they want to escape, we first have to understand the types of BPD and how they intersect with addiction.

There is a relationship between these two struggles that goes beyond a simple cause-and-effect. It reflects deeper questions about identity, managing pain, and a human need for stability. The way BPD manifests can determine not only how someone experiences their internal world, but which substances they turn to, and why. These distinctions are essential to break free from the cycle of emotional dysregulation and addiction.

Four Patterns Common Across the Multiple Types of BPD

Because each person is unique, borderline personality disorder doesn’t present the same way in everyone. Four primary patterns help explain the different ways that BPD manifests. These types of BPD are not meant to box people into categories concretely, but rather, they help us understand the ways emotional dysregulation shows up in real life. By recognizing which patterns resonate most with an individual, Christian counselors can guide treatment and offer hope that recovery is possible.

The discouraged type: This form of BPD often appears in people who seem dependent and seek constant reassurance while struggling with feelings of worthlessness. These individuals may appear passive or submissive in relationships and avoid confrontation, even when it would be healthy.

The impulsive type: Those who manifest this type of BPD often engage in risk-taking behaviors and emotional outbursts without concern for consequences. People who struggle with this form of BPT typically act on every feeling without pausing to consider the outcome, and they chase experiences that provide immediate gratification or distraction from inner emptiness.

The petulant type: This form of BPD involves stubborn negativity and feeling misunderstood, which results in pushing others away by simultaneously fearing abandonment. Individuals struggling with this pattern often feel like victims of their circumstances and may express bitterness or resentment toward those trying to help.

The self-destructive type: This pattern of BPD manifests in harmful behaviors directed inward, which include substance abuse, self-harm, or extreme risk-taking to manage unbearable emotional pain. Individuals of this type are the most visibly concerning. They seem intent on destroying themselves, even though self-harm isn’t about wanting to die. It’s about making internal pain visible.

Each of these patterns reflects a different strategy for managing the emotional dysregulation that is at the heart of BPD. Many individuals display characteristics from multiple types, and patterns can shift over time, so these categories are not considered rigid.

The consistency across these patterns is the intense fear of abandonment, unstable self-image, and difficulty regulating emotions that define the disorder. Adding substance abuse to this already intense struggle starts as an attempt to navigate the emotional turbulence that feels impossible to manage any other way.

Why Substance Abuse Co-Occurs with BPD

The connection between BPD and addiction is not coincidental. Most individuals diagnosed with BPD also struggle with substance use disorders. Because BPD creates an emotionally intense environment, substances often offer temporary relief from these struggles.

An individual experiencing rapid mood swings, chronic feelings of emptiness, and a fear of abandonment turns to alcohol or other substances to quiet the internal chaos. Substances only provide a brief escape from emotions that feel overwhelming and unmanageable.

Self-medication is not the only challenge with substance abuse and BPD. The brain chemistry is changed due to substance use, which can worsen BPD symptoms and create a cycle where each issue amplifies the other. Impulsivity is a core feature of BPD, and it can become more pronounced under the influence of substances, and emotional regulation becomes nearly impossible.

Christian counselors recognize that both conditions require integrated treatment. They emphasize that addressing one only leaves the underlying vulnerabilities untouched. The path to healing requires understanding how these struggles reinforce each other and learning how to cultivate healthier ways to cope with emotional pain. One good place to start is with encouraging Scriptures:

Cast your burden upon the Lord and He will sustain you; He will never allow the righteous to be shaken. – Psalm 55:22, NASB

How Different Types of BPD Influence Substance Use Patterns

A specific pattern of BPD often shapes the relationship an individual has with substances. Impulsive-type individuals engage in binge drinking or experiment with multiple substances, trying to find a thrill and temporary relief from boredom or inner emptiness.

Individuals who struggle with the self-destructive type of BPD may use substances deliberately to harm themselves or engage in dangerous combinations of risky behaviors. They are less concerned with pleasure and more focused on punishing themselves or numbing severe emotional pain.

Individuals who struggle with the discouraged type often use substances to cope with feelings of hopelessness and inadequacy. Using substances becomes an internal coping mechanism to numb the discouraging feelings.

The individual who suffers from the petulant type of BPD faces a more complex dynamic when it comes to substance use. They may engage in substance use in response to a perceived rejection or conflict. The result is a pattern where relationship struggles trigger substance use, which creates more relationship problems.

Christian counselors understand these patterns and can develop treatment approaches that address the specific needs of each individual who struggles with substance use and BPD. The goal is to build healthier ways to manage emotional experiences that made substances feel necessary in the first place.

Still, we are all reminded of Jesus’ words:

“Come to Me, all who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.” – Matthew 11:28, NASB

The Path Toward Integrated Healing

Co-occurring BPD and substance abuse recovery requires addressing both conditions simultaneously. If BPD remains untreated, traditional addiction treatment fails because the emotional dysregulation continues to drive the compulsion toward substances.

On the other hand, if BPD is treated without addressing active addiction, the treatment is ineffective because substances interfere with the ability to develop healthy coping strategies. Through integrated treatment, individuals learn to recognize that these conditions exist in relationship to one another and must be addressed together.

Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) has become an effective treatment plan for individuals dealing with both BPD and substance abuse. Through this approach, individuals learn specific skills to manage distress, tolerate stress, and build more effective relationships.

Christian counselors often integrate faith-based perspectives and evidence-based treatments to help clients understand their value in Christ as they develop practical tools to manage symptoms. This process involves learning that emotions do not have to be escaped or numbed. Even intense emotions can be experienced, understood, and regulated in healthy ways.

Finding the Support You Need

The relationship between BPD and substance abuse is a reflection of a human tendency to seek relief from pain through whatever feels available. For treatment to be effective, individuals must understand the different patterns of BPD and how they intersect with addiction.

Each type of BPD – the discouraged, the impulsive, the petulant, or the self-destructive – presents a unique challenge and strength in the recovery process. The consistency is the need for integrated treatment that addresses both the emotional dysregulation involved with BPD and addictive patterns.

Healthy recovery includes building new skills, developing healthier coping mechanisms, and discovering that lasting peace isn’t found by escaping emotions. Instead, you can learn to navigate feelings with grace, support, and God’s Word.

If you or someone you know is facing the complex challenges of BPD and substance abuse, professional support can make a meaningful difference in your recovery. Christian counselors are trained to integrate faith-based encouragement with evidence-based treatment to help you navigate this journey and find lasting recovery.

Reach out to our office and connect with a Christian counselor who can help you take the first step toward integrated care for these struggles.

item.title: What Moral Scrupulosity Feels Like
item.description:
It’s admirable when people strive to be decent and morally upstanding, especially when they are setting an example to others. However, sometimes there is something sinister and overwhelming that drives certain people to be good. Moral scrupulosity is a type of Obsessive Compulsive Disorder (OCD) that urges a person to become intensely preoccupied with being a good person.

Sadly, it also causes a person to feel extreme anxiety, guilt, shame, exhaustion, and fear of being exposed as a fraud. It is as if they have a voice in their head constantly criticizing their actions, shining a spotlight on their mistakes, and making their small errors feel like unforgivable sins.

Being a decent person takes effort, and it’s not always easy to make the right choices. However, moral OCD causes intense distortions in a person’s view of themselves. Even a person who has a solid reputation can end up feeling like a moral failure because of the intrusive thoughts that surround moral OCD.

As with all forms of Obsessive Compulsive Disorder, it is possible to treat moral scrupulosity. First, however, you must understand how and to what extent it is affecting you.

Not Just About People-Pleasing

On the surface of things, moral scrupulosity often looks a lot like people-pleasing. People-pleasers need more than the average amount of reassurance from others, and the same is true for those with moral OCD. Both people-pleasers and those with moral scrupulosity try to keep others happy, and both want to be seen as kind, thoughtful, generous, and decent. The difference lies in their inner monologue and motivations.

People-pleasers feel the need to make others happy and to keep the peace in every environment. They will compromise their boundaries, disregard their personal preferences, and allow themselves to be taken advantage of to a degree. However, people pleasers do not experience the same inner monologue and intrusive thoughts as those with OCD. Also, people-pleasing habits greatly differ from OCD compulsions.

Moral scrupulosity hijacks a person’s conscience and takes over their actions. As with other kinds of OCD, there is a voice in their head constantly criticizing and challenging them to do certain things, or ridiculing them for not doing certain things.

For example, something as simple as drinking from a plastic straw can spark internal turmoil for someone with moral OCD. A people-pleaser might feel a twinge of guilt for the environment while sipping from a plastic straw. A person with moral scrupulosity will inwardly berate themselves for hours, framing this simple act as hypocrisy and moral failure.

What Moral Scrupulosity Sounds Like

There are two components to every type of obsessive compulsive disorder: intrusive thoughts and ritualistic or habitual actions. Moral scrupulosity is a ridiculing, criticizing, and sometimes threatening inner voice that spurs panic, fear, anxiety, and shame. It might be an echo of someone you know, or it might take on the quality of your own voice, but more cruel.

You will have thoughts like, “Who do you think you are, pretending to be like this?” or “You are being fake, and everyone will notice.” Sometimes your efforts will be singled out, and you will have thoughts like, “No matter what you do, you will never reach the standards you should,” or “You should have felt worse about that.”

None of these thoughts comes anything close to being positive, encouraging, or uplifting, and only results in you feeling worse about yourself. Most of them will have you questioning your self-worth, and some will cause you to wonder if you are a sociopath, a narcissist, or something worse.

Moral Scrupulosity in Action

Moral OCD mostly exists in your head. As with all OCD, the intrusive thoughts frequently lead to compulsive behavior and ritualistic habits. Many of these habits don’t appear to be obsessive or compulsive, but they are connected to the feelings that come from moral scrupulosity.

Some of the most common habits connected to moral scrupulosity are confessing, apologizing, and seeking reassurance. Feeling constantly guilty or on the verge of moral failure will lead you to scramble in an effort to save your reputation or prove your worth. You might have constant conversations with your spouse, partner, confidante, or pastor about your failures, or you might obsessively journal your fears and anxieties.

With moral OCD, you likely replay conversations over in your head, especially if you hurt someone with your words or were dishonest about something. Even when you feel as if you performed well socially, you still review your words and actions.

You will search for flaws, mistakes, or breaches of social etiquette, which you will use to berate yourself afterwards. These performance reviews become a ritual of sorts after any interaction or conversation you have.

Sometimes you will feel compelled to balance the scales with your actions. For example, in penitence for drinking from a plastic straw, you might donate more money than you can afford to a wildlife rescue fund. Actions like these, while hardly ever practical, become important ways for you to prove your morality and challenge your hypocrisy. They are also a way for you to punish personal wrongdoing and prove that you have leveled up your inner goodness.

Besides having a harsh inner-monitoring system, engaging in costly good deeds, and feeling compelled to confess your wrongdoing constantly, moral scrupulosity also leads to rigid rule-keeping. For you, rules are less about maintaining order or discipline and more about heavy ethics and social purity.

Guidelines become commandments, and failure on your behalf to comply with the code is an intense moral failing that you will struggle to repent from. You will likely also avoid getting involved in anything that feels morally gray or ambiguous. This leads you to pass up certain job opportunities, relationships, or hobbies if they seem like they will lead down a morally dubious path.

Free To Fail

As with all forms of OCD, moral scrupulosity is treatable with certain therapies. Forefront among these is Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and Exposure and Response Prevention (ERP). Recognizing the impact of your thoughts and actions is the start, and from there, you must be willing to feel uncomfortable as your worldview and belief system are challenged.

Recovery from moral OCD can only be gradual. You cannot change intrusive thoughts and compulsive actions overnight, nor would it be healthy if you could. CBT challenges the inner beliefs that surround moral scrupulosity, and ERP exposes you to different thoughts and challenges you to try new actions in response to them.

At first, it is unnerving to replace automatic thoughts like “I am a terrible person” with new thoughts like “Even when I make a mistake, I remain a decent person.” In time, your reflexive thoughts and actions begin to shift, and you will find yourself less preoccupied with your own failures and more focused on your triumphs and breakthroughs.

Somewhere out there, faith exists without fear, and love overrides guilt. Grace is not simply a concept applicable to other people who have earned it. Grace is a force that changes those who are most in need of it and most undeserving of it. Although it might be hard to believe, life does not have to be this difficult forever. Not only are you capable of change, but you are worthy of it.

Dealing with any type of OCD is overwhelming. Simply knowing you have an issue is only the start; now you must get help for it.

We host an online catalog that lists the details of many different counselors, where we hope you will find someone who can help you. If you would prefer to speak with people to arrange a meeting with a counselor, our reception team would love to help you. We hope you will find someone who can help you recover from OCD for good.

item.title: Chronic Loneliness and the Quiet Ache of Feeling Unseen
item.description:
Feeling invisible in a room full of people can leave you feeling disoriented. Whether it’s at a family gathering, a church service, or lunch with coworkers, something inside of you feels completely cut off from everyone around you. This isn’t a passing mood or a signal that you need a quiet evening at home. For most individuals, it’s a daily reality of chronic loneliness, even amid a busy schedule and a calendar full of social events.

There are no convenient moments for chronic loneliness to show up, but it is there, quiet and persistent, in places and circumstances that are supposed to feel the opposite of alone. This type of loneliness is difficult to address because it rarely looks like loneliness should. It’s not someone sitting alone with nowhere to go and no one to call.

Chronic loneliness is something different. It often affects people who are engaged, busy, and surrounded by family, church, and community. It is the hidden disconnection they feel underneath all of that activity. The first step in healing is to name it. Then, understanding follows, and healing can begin. Even Scripture encourages people to be honest about their loneliness:

Turn to me and be gracious to me, for I am lonely and afflicted. – Psalm 25:16, ESV

The Silence That Lives Inside a Crowded Room

It doesn’t seem right that it works this way; more people should mean more connections. Sitting in church pews with familiar faces or showing up to social events can still make people feel as though they are strangers in spaces where they should feel at home.

This issue goes far beyond not having people nearby. It includes something hard to name: a persistent sense that no one truly sees you, knows you, or notices if you come undone on the inside. This type of absence is more isolating than physical solitude could ever be.

We have societal expectations that shape this experience in ways we don’t always notice. A prevailing attitude that suggests that if you’re actively involved in a rooted community, especially a faith community, you should be fine. This generates an invisible pressure to perform kindness, even when the inside does not match the outside. People learn to smile, show up, and keep participating while feeling disconnected from the environments that foster belonging.

Christian counselors recognize this pattern before people are ready to acknowledge the loneliness outright. They show up exhausted, emotionally flat, and unsure, while nothing feels like it is working anymore. Proverbs 14 identifies this juxtaposition: “Even in laughter the heart may ache, and the end of joy may be grief.” (Proverbs 14:13, ESV)

What Chronic Loneliness Looks Like Beneath the Surface

Chronic loneliness is not a reflection of how many relationships you have. People can surround you, and you can still experience deep, persistent isolation. It is the distinction that matters, because it shifts the focus away from external circumstances toward the internal experience.

That experience is the quality of connection, the sense of genuinely being known, and the emotional safety that you feel in your relationships. When these elements are absent, a void registers in your body and mind, and it is difficult to ignore. It shows up as a quiet sense that something important is missing, and it is accompanied by emotional numbness.

There are social pressures that shape how you connect with others, and they contribute to this far more than you recognize. Competing values around being self-sufficient, productive, and having things together make it difficult to admit there’s something wrong.

Admitting loneliness is like admitting failure, especially in places of faith, where community has value and expectations. The result is a cycle that is difficult to break because of the avoidance of vulnerability. Pulling back deepens the disconnection that you’re trying to manage quietly, and the outcome is a persistent, unnamed suffering that rarely surfaces until something breaks open. Even in these lonely, broken places, you can hold onto the truth that God is near.

The Lord is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit. – Psalm 34:18, ESV

What Faith Says About Feeling This Type of Aloneness

God’s Word does not pretend that loneliness is not real. There are many honest prayers in the Bible that come from people who felt utterly isolated, such as prophets, kings in hiding, and disciples scattered by fear. The book of Psalms is filled with raw and unpolished cries that name emptiness and abandonment without any apology or qualification.

This is significant because it reminds us that profound loneliness is not a sign of insufficient faith or spiritual weakness. It is simply a human experience that God never asked anyone to minimize, deny, or quietly push through alone. God has always been acquainted with this kind of grief.

Faith does not offer an immediate answer to the ache, but it brings a genuine presence with it. God entered the human experience through Christ, and that His darkest hour was marked by complete abandonment. This doesn’t remove the pain of loneliness; instead, it gives it a witness. The experience of being unseen has already been brought before God, and He did not look away.

When you can bring your disconnection honestly before God and before a trusted community, something shifts. Christian counselors recognize that the intersection of spiritual and emotional health is central to their work. You cannot address the mind without addressing the spirit and expect it to be a lasting change.

Finding Your Way From Chronic Loneliness To Real Connection

Navigating chronic loneliness is not quick, and it is never linear. It requires that you learn to identify what a genuine connection actually feels like, not what it is supposed to look like from the outside. It is understanding what truly leaves you feeling less invisible and more fully yourself.

This process may include grieving the relationships and environments that were unable to offer that kind of safety. It is no secret that grief and loneliness are closely related. It will take patience and honest self-reflection to begin separating one from the other without losing sight of either.

When you reach out to a counselor, a trusted person in your community, or to God in prayer, that is the hardest and most important step. You can then move directly against the social pressure to handle things privately and maintain the appearance of self-sufficiency. This becomes the beginning of something real.

Christian counselors can help you examine the relational patterns that have kept you isolated and understand where those patterns developed. Then you can begin building toward the kind of connection that actually holds. Faith won’t ask you to be fine. It will ask you to be honest, and in that honesty is the very thing that interrupts the cycle.

Don’t Go Through This Alone

Chronic loneliness in the middle of a full life is a quiet form of pain that rarely announces itself and rarely receives the attention it deserves. This loneliness lives beneath conversations and behind smiles, hidden inside of people who have become quite practiced at looking fine while feeling far away from almost everyone around them. It is real, it matters, and it doesn’t have to remain a permanent aspect of your daily life.

There is nothing about your loneliness that disqualifies you from connection, community, or the nearness of God. He has never stopped moving toward the isolated and unseen. The journey toward connection begins with naming what is actually true. That means deciding to stop carrying what was never designed to be carried alone.

Whether you speak with a Christian counselor, reach out to someone you trust, sit in prayer, or acknowledge the weight of what you’ve been quietly holding, that is the beginning. And every beginning is always worth the step.

If loneliness has become a familiar or persistent part of your daily life, you do not have to face it alone. You can reach out to our office today and talk with our reception team to get started on your journey toward something better.

item.title: The Smile that Hides Repressed Anger
item.description:
Sometimes anger can convince people that it’s not there. It doesn’t always come with a loud voice in a heated moment. It can roll in quietly, disguised as a tight jaw, sudden irritability, or a withdrawn spirit. Repressed anger is a deceptive emotion that many people carry.

By the time it’s recognized, it’s been living under the surface for months, and it no longer feels like anger. It has been shaping decisions and relationships for months or even years in ways that are hard to trace back to the source. Scripture has clear guidelines on anger:

In your anger do not sin: Do not let the sun go down while you are still angry. – Ephesians 4:26, NIV

The Bible tells us that we will experience anger, but it’s what we do in that anger that creates the struggles and issues. Repressed anger is deeper than a spiritual choice. Managing anger by keeping it out of sight and holding it at a distance can be the underlying assumption in faith communities. But now we are coming to understand that this is not handling it well and that the hidden anger carries real weight.

What Repressed Anger Really Looks Like

Repressed anger doesn’t identify itself by a name. It tends to present as persistent, low-grade sadness or unexplained irritability. It could be a withdrawal from once meaningful relationships.

This surfaces when people have spent years managing emotional responses for the sake of others, leading them to lose touch with what they’re actually feeling beneath the surface. By the time the anger surfaces, it may have been buried so long that the person no longer recognizes it for what it is.

Each individual has a choice to establish internal honesty. It’s not comfortable, but it is necessary for understanding how we manage emotional responses. In places that feel complicated or unflattering, an individual can begin to know themselves fully. Faith communities tend to suggest that certain emotions make self-examination a spiritual risk.

When individuals or communities have framed anger as a sign of spiritual immaturity or something that a truly trusting person doesn’t experience, honesty becomes difficult to access. Just because an emotion isn’t acknowledged doesn’t mean it disappears. It just learns to live quietly until it can’t anymore.

Search me, God, and know my heart; test me and know my anxious thoughts. See if there is any offensive way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting. – Psalm 139:23-24, NIV

The Hidden Cost of Keeping the Peace

Sometimes peace is a cover for avoidance, wearing a spiritual name. This happens when it involves staying quiet even though something genuinely needs to be said or moving past a wound before it has been addressed honestly. Surface-level peacemaking results in something that looks like patience but functions like suppression. The result is a calm exterior that pushes down everything that’s never been allowed to be named.

Anger does not have to be dissolved before it is examined to show emotional maturity. Wisdom in handling emotions comes from understanding the difference between unrestrained anger and engaging with what has been building beneath the surface.

Christian counselors help individuals who have chosen suppression over engagement, or who have lived under the belief that burying difficult emotions was the faithful choice. The process of understanding repressed anger begins with realizing that it does not protect a person. It only delays what will need to be addressed at a greater cost.

Repressed Anger and the Body’s Honest Response

Emotional suppression and physical health have a well-documented connection, especially when it comes to anger. The body will respond over time when anger has been withheld rather than processed. It shows up in chronic muscle tension, recurring headaches, digestive difficulties, and disrupted sleep.

The body was not created to absorb what the mind refuses to examine. It will register what is carried and communicate it in ways that become increasingly hard to ignore as the body reveals hidden issues through outward symptoms.

God’s Word offers straightforward instruction to be slow to anger, but there is a deeper meaning in this instruction than first appears. When an individual is slowed to anger, they adopt a posture that reflects thoughtfulness, reflection, and a willingness to listen before reacting. This is the opposite of suppression, which bypasses reflection entirely and buries the emotion without engagement.

Christian counselors can help individuals focus on the intersection of faith and emotional health by helping clients distinguish between the responses of suppression and reflection. Suppression is not being slow to anger. It is avoidance. Whatever an individual consistently avoids will find other ways to make itself known, whether through physical symptoms, relationships, or behavior.

My dear brothers and sisters, take note of this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak and slow to become angry, because human anger does not produce the righteousness that God desires. – James 1:19-20, NIV

Finding Honest Ground Between Repressed Anger and Real Healing

When an individual moves away from the belief that their emotions are a spiritual problem and toward the understanding that the emotions carry spiritual information, they experience a meaningful shift. Anger often points to something real, even when it is buried. It indicates there was a boundary that was crossed, a wound that was minimized by others, or a loss that was never fully grieved.

Christian counselors recognize this shift and can help individuals name and grapple with the repressed anger that leads to an honest foundation where true healing can take place. Jesus never suggested that an offense be minimized or set aside.

He named it in a way that extends beyond interpersonal conflict. It reaches into the inner work of honestly acknowledging what has been dismissed or left untouched. Reconciliation requires honesty, whether it’s with oneself or with others.

The resolve to deal with what has been left unresolved isn’t a detour from faith, but rather wisdom in action. Many individuals find that their faith comes alive and is practical when they are honest about the repressed anger hidden beneath the surface.

Discover the Peace You Long For

People often smile when they don’t have the language or feel safe enough to do anything else. A smile is intended to be a reflection of wholeness that comes from the outward and inward life aligning. God’s Word does not ask people to perform emotionally. He invites them to genuine peace formed through honest engagement with Him in the reality of personal experience. This includes the parts that have been living quietly beneath the surface.

Jesus describes a peace that is not built on suppressing what is difficult, or on pretending that it’s not there. This peace comes to those who fully acknowledge what they carry. Those who are moving through the process of naming a long-buried emotion and following it to its source move into a place of honest healing. This isn’t a deficit of faith or the lack of it, but it can be how faith comes alive from the inside out.

Peace I leave with you; my peace I give you. I do not give to you as the world gives. Do not let your hearts be troubled and do not be afraid. – John 14:27, NIV

If you think you may struggle with repressed anger, you don’t have to suppress it any longer. You don’t have to navigate the journey of understanding that anger alone. Contact our office and speak with our reception team to make an appointment. They will connect you with support that will help you navigate mental health and faith honestly.

item.title: Is It Possible for Kids to Control their Emotions? A Child Therapist Weighs In
item.description:
Upon asking if it is possible for kids to control their emotions, it is equally important to ask whether it is reasonable to expect it. As a therapist who has worked with children five years old and older, I will answer yes to both questions. Yes, it is possible for kids to control their emotions. And yes, it is reasonable to expect a child five years old to be able to control their emotions.

However, defining what that control means and looks like is key to understanding how it will look in operation and function in a child. Controlling emotions refers to the ability to identify, steward, and respond to emotional stimulation in a balanced or healthy way versus dismissing or ignoring them. Controlling emotions in therapeutic terms is referred to as emotional regulation.

Emotional regulation is the process of managing the intensity, duration, and expression of emotions to respond correctly to situations while maintaining mental well-being. Note that this definition does not intend for the child to avoid or repress the feelings that arise but requires them to manage their emotional reaction.

Emotional reaction management helps ensure that decision-making does not become overwhelmed and that social interactions remain mostly positive.

Every Child Can Learn About Emotions

Per the National Center for Education Statistics, children can learn more about their emotions than we sometimes give them credit for. Even young children are taking in information, remembering patterns, and beginning to connect what they feel with what is happening around them. By ages 2-3, children can begin holding on to information in meaningful ways.

As they move closer to ages 4-5, their memory, attention, and ability to follow simple steps continue to grow. This matters because emotional regulation is also learned step by step. A child may not always respond perfectly, but with consistent teaching, modeling, and practice, they can learn to pause, name what they feel, and choose a safer or more appropriate response.

Teaching children emotional regulation requires teaching them in a way they can comprehend. Children need the concept of “emotional regulation” broken down into a more understandable construct such as “pause and check in.” Often, taking the foundational meaning of words and using them with a younger mind helps them better connect with meaning.

Emotional regulation at its foundation is all about pausing and checking in with yourself first. Although emotional regulation is profoundly serious, allowing a child to learn emotional regulation by making it into a “tag-your-it” type of game is okay.

As a therapist who has worked with children and adolescents, the intensity can be lessened if fun can be had. However, always remind the child that fun is okay, and safety is the best friend of fun. We can have fun if you are safe, and so is everyone else. This is layered, but it is the step-by-step method that was previously mentioned. Once you convey the concept, begin to build on it to add other important ideas regarding emotional regulation.

What A Child Needs to Know About Their Emotions

The first thing that a child needs to know about their emotions is that they are not bad, stupid, make them an annoying person, make them weird, should make them feel scared, or any other negative conclusion they may have come to.

Children must know that emotions are a part of their human experience and their emotions are God given. The goal is to help them not only regulate their emotions but to understand them so that they can avoid shame or even embarrassment because of what they are feeling.

Here are a few simple phrases that can help children and adolescents feel seen, supported, and less alone in what they are experiencing.

  • “It’s okay to not feel okay.” – Normalizes odd feelings without judgement.
  • “Sadness can feel lonely. Can I sit with you quietly?” – Normalize maintaining connecting during tough times versus isolation.
  • “Crying is okay. I will get you some tissue.” – The focus is getting the child comfortable with being supported while being validated (seen).
  • “Feeling scared is hard. What do you need right now? – The focus is getting the child to speak to how to name what would meet their need, by using their words.

The key is to keep it simple, continue step-by-step and to model. Children need to see that we not only understand but are present. Being present is not just about our bodies being in the same space, meaning proximity. They need to know that an adult is present in their eyes and with their hearts. This matters to any child in any emotional state at any time.

Modeling is one of the most effective ways children learn emotional regulation. Children are always watching how the adults around them respond to frustration, sadness, disappointment, fear, and even joy.

When adults can slow down, name what is happening, and respond steadily, children begin to learn that emotions can be felt without taking over the whole moment. This is not about being perfect in front of a child. It is about allowing the child to see regulation practiced in real time.

One Step Further

The goal is to build a foundation of understanding not only emotional regulation but to also take it one step further to begin establishing good mental health. Think about that for a second, what if it was widespread practice to put into place the building blocks for children to have a good headstart to sound mental health.

Children who understand their emotions grow into adults who understand their emotions as well as how to manage them. Children can control their emotions when they learn that their emotions are a part of their human experience.

As a therapist who is a Christian, I can tell you that unpacking that truth, along with the reality that God equipped us with emotions for a purpose, and that they are good. God speaks of emotions and how to manage them throughout His Word.

A child must know that anger is real and God is aware. Fear is going to show up; God knew it and warned us that we were going to have to stand up to fear, not run from it. With God’s help, they can emotionally regulate.

Children are easy to teach when we know what we are teaching and how to teach it. When controlling emotions is taught with consideration of self, others, environment, and outcome, it helps to create step-by-step instruction, which creates consistency in demonstration and modeling.

As children grow into adolescents the emotional lessons that they learn will undoubtedly stick with them while allowing additional knowledge of more complicated emotional concepts.

Sensitivity can be learned, and due to our culture, which is heavily packed with less-kind television programming, video games, and movie entertainment, sensitivity is an emotion we cannot afford to leave children to gather on their own.

Teaching children how to manage anger and express it in a healthy way is a necessity our current society can no longer ignore. Ignoring emotional health until it becomes a crisis. When a child is in mental crisis, there is less chance of helping them, and it is harder to assist the appointed adult with comprehending what is happening with them in the moment.

The more clarity that can be given to children to help them identify and understand their emotions, the better we can help them manage what they go through while continuing to understand who they are and will become emotionally.

item.title: Beauty from Ashes: God’s Healing Work Through Heartbreak and Loss
item.description:
To all who mourn in Israel, he will give a crown of beauty for ashes, a joyous blessing instead of mourning, festive praise instead of despair. In their righteousness, they will be like great oaks that the LORD has planted for his own glory. –  Isaiah 61:3, NLT

Everyone experiences disappointment. At some point in life, we all encounter heartbreak, loss, betrayal, rejection, or circumstances that leave us wondering how we will ever move forward. We live in a fallen world, and the world has a way of letting us down. People fail us. Dreams don’t unfold as planned. Doors close unexpectedly. Life doesn’t always deliver what we hoped for.

Giving Heartbreak to God

What do we do with those feelings? How do we respond when life seems to fall apart?

…we know that God causes everything to work together for the good of those who love God and are called according to his purpose for them. – Romans 8:28, NLT

Notice that Scripture says everything – not just the victories, blessings, and successes. God works through the failures, disappointments, losses, and painful seasons as well. The very things that seem to derail us often become the path through which God accomplishes His purposes.

Over the years, both my husband and I have experienced firsthand what it means for God to bring beauty from ashes. Though our stories are different, they share a common theme: what felt like devastation became the place where God was at work, redeeming what once seemed lost. Looking back, we can both see Romans 8:28 and Isaiah 61:3 woven throughout our journeys.

Ten years ago, a significant event occurred that changed the course of both my life and my marriage. I found myself in a deep, dark place. It felt as though my world was crashing down around me. I thought the life I knew was over.

Yet even in that darkness, I sensed God’s presence. Though I couldn’t see how things would work out, I held on to the promise that He would somehow redeem what felt broken. I clung to the hope found in Isaiah 61:3 – that God could bring beauty from ashes, joy from mourning, and praise from despair. One year later, God gave me a visual. I kept seeing flowers, plants, or other vegetation blooming through volcanic ash or solidified lava.

Think about a volcanic eruption. At the moment, it leaves nothing but devastation. Everything in its path is buried, burned, or destroyed. It appears hopeless. Yet God designed creation so that even volcanic destruction can become the foundation for new life. The ash and minerals enrich the soil. Over time, new growth emerges. Entire ecosystems are reborn, sometimes more vibrant than before.

As the anniversary of that painful season approached, I found myself reflecting on how far God had brought me. While traces of old grief occasionally surfaced, I could clearly see His faithfulness. Just like those small plants pushing through the ash, God had been restoring me and our marriage – piece by piece.

Around that same time, several worship songs seemed to echo the message God was teaching me. One song reminded me that we were “made to rise” above difficult circumstances. Another spoke of how God often uses people with scars rather than those who appear perfect. Yet another declared, “I see shattered, You see whole. I see broken, but You see beautiful.”

Those lyrics resonated deeply because they reflected what God had been doing in my life. What looked ruined wasn’t beyond His reach. What felt lost wasn’t wasted.

That season was marked by betrayal, loss, and the challenging work of rebuilding. Yet looking back, I can see Romans 8:28 in action. God did not waste the pain. He used it and made things better than they were before.

The Bible and Heartbreak

Many people struggle with disappointment because they expect life, relationships, careers, or circumstances to fulfill something only God can provide. The world continually promises satisfaction yet repeatedly falls short.

From a counseling perspective, disappointment often carries secondary emotions that people don’t immediately recognize. Beneath the sadness may be grief. Beneath the anger may be hurt. Beneath the fear may be a sense of lost identity or unmet expectations. Many people become stuck because they try to push those feelings down or away rather than acknowledge them.

Healing rarely happens by pretending we are unaffected by our circumstances. Healing begins when we honestly bring our pain before God, allow ourselves to process what has been lost, and trust Him to work it out for good.

Scripture is filled with examples of people who grieved, lamented, questioned, and struggled. Yet their stories remind us that pain and faith can coexist. We do not have to choose between trusting God and being honest about our disappointment.

The Bible also powerfully illustrates how God redeems human adversity and hardships by consistently transforming trials, tribulations, pain, and adversity into ultimate good for those who love Him. This fundamental promise provides believers with the assurance that every aspect of their story has a purpose under God’s divine guidance. Perhaps that disappointment serves a greater purpose than we realize.

If you are navigating a difficult season and finding it hard to see beyond the pain, Christian counseling may be a helpful resource. A trained Christian counselor can help you process emotions, identify unhealthy patterns, strengthen coping skills, and explore how biblical truth applies to your unique circumstances. While counseling cannot remove the hardship, it can provide support, encouragement, and practical tools as you move toward healing and restoration.

Romans 8

Recently, my husband shared a similar message with the young adults at our church. As I read his notes, I realized how closely they connected with what God had taught both of us through our own difficult seasons.

He reminded them, “The world disappoints – it lets you down. But Romans 8:28 reframes every letdown as something God is actively working through for your good.” He called it “The Beautiful Letdown.” He explained that the “letdown” becomes the vehicle of God’s purpose. When we look closely at Romans 8:28, we see several powerful truths:

“All things” – This is not just the victories, but the failures, rejections, and disappointments. The moments where the world didn’t deliver. Those moments – the letdowns – are actually where something real is happening.

“Work for the good” – The letdown isn’t wasted. God takes the very thing that hurt or disappointed you and uses it redemptively.

  • The dissatisfaction we feel with this world is not necessarily a spiritual problem – it can be a gift. It keeps us from settling for temporary things and reminds us that we were created for something more.
  • When you’re dissatisfied with the world, it keeps you focused on more important things.
  • This place isn’t our home…we’re just passing through en route to a better place.

“Called according to his purpose” – this is why the letdown is beautiful. You were called to something beyond what this world offers. The disappointment is confirmation that you belong somewhere else.

The world will always let you down, and that’s exactly what God uses to keep your eyes on Him. There is only One who will never let you down or disappoint you: God.

Revelation 21:4 NLT tells us, “He will wipe every tear from their eyes, and there will be no more death or sorrow or crying or pain. All these things are gone forever.”

  • The beautiful letdown is Romans 8:28 in experience.
  • What felt like loss was actually God working.
  • What felt like rejection was redirection.
  • What felt like the world closing a door was God reminding you that this was never your home to begin with.

Looking back now, we can clearly see God’s hand at work in what once felt like complete devastation. For my husband, exactly one year after his painful season, he met me – the woman who would become his wife. Today, we have been married for thirty-one years.

Years later, during one of the most painful seasons of our marriage, I experienced my own “beauty from ashes” story. Instead of walking away, we made the decision to fight for our marriage rather than fight with each other.

In both of our stories, what once felt like ashes became something beautiful. What felt like an ending became a new beginning. And through it all, God proved Himself faithful. What once looked like ashes became a testimony of His grace, reminding us that He truly does give beauty for ashes.
